content: The United States Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry is a legislative body within the Senate that oversees all matters related to agriculture, farming programs, forestry, and nutrition. It was established in 1825 following a proposal by Senator William Findlay of Pennsylvania, who argued that agriculture was as vital to national progress as commerce and manufacturing. The Senate agreed to divide the Committee on Commerce and Manufactures into two separate entities, leading to the creation of the Committee on Agriculture on December 9, 1825. During its early years, the necessity of the committee was frequently questioned, as agriculture-related issues often overlapped with the jurisdiction of other committees. At the time, nearly two-thirds of the U.S. population was directly involved in agriculture, which led to many agricultural matters being referred to other committees. In 1857, a Special Committee recommended reorganizing Senate committees to improve efficiency, which resulted in the dissolution of the Agriculture Committee on March 5, 1857. In 1862, amidst the Civil War, increasing immigration, and the nation’s shift toward industrialization, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Organic Act, which reestablished the Department of Agriculture. In 1884, the committee was renamed the Committee on Agriculture and Forestry to reflect the growing importance of forestry to the nation. In 1977, the committee was renamed again to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, following the Food and Agriculture Act of 1977. This legislation directed the Department of Agriculture to expand its focus on human nutrition research, establish a national nutrition education program, and develop a system to monitor the nutritional status of Americans. As of the 110th Congress, the committee was chaired by Senator Tom Harkin, a Democrat from Iowa, with Senator Saxby Chambliss, a Republican from Georgia, serving as the Ranking Minority Member. The committee is divided into five subcommittees, each focusing on specific areas: Nutrition and Food Assistance, Sustainable and Organic Agriculture, and General Legislation; Energy, Science, and Technology; Domestic and Foreign Marketing, Inspection, and Plant and Animal Health; Production, Income Protection, and Price Support; and Rural Revitalization, Conservation, Forestry, and Credit. The committee has had a long history of leadership, with its chairmanship evolving over time. From 1829 to 1857, notable chairmen included William Marks, Horatio Seymour, and Bedford Brown. After its reestablishment in 1863, leaders such as John Sherman, Simon Cameron, and Oliver P. Morton guided the committee. From 1884 to 1977, during its tenure as the Committee on Agriculture and Forestry, chairmen included Warner Miller, Redfield Proctor, and Ellison D. Smith. Since 1977, under its current name, the committee has been led by figures such as Herman E. Talmadge, Jesse Helms, Patrick Leahy, and Richard G. Lugar. As of the most recent information, Senator Tom Harkin continues to serve as chairman.
